title: Per-token Utility Scorer: INT8/FP8/4-bit Workbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight workbook / thought doc for a per-token utility scoring approach to decide quantization level at request time. Goal: give SREs / SDKs a simple decision surface to route or transcode requests between FP16/FP8/INT8/4-bit (or hybrid) to optimize cost while bounding expected quality degradation and meeting latency SLOs.

Summary (tl;dr):
- Instead of a single global quant profile, compute an approximate expected utility-per-token (UPT) for each incoming request class and pick the minimal-cost quant level whose expected UPT loss is below an application-specific tolerance.
- UPT combines: value_of_correctness (business weight for output quality), predicted tokens_generated, model-sensitivity factor (empirical fidelity loss curve), and latency/cost multipliers.
- Prototype scoring formula and worked examples below; spreadsheet tabs suggested: "Input profiles", "Sensitivity curves", "UPT simulation", "Routing rules", "Backtest".

Key motivations & constraints:
- Many customers have mixed workloads: short transactional prompts (high value per token) + long generation tasks (lower marginal value). A single quant configuration wastes economic opportunity.
- Quantization interacts with sequence length and beam/temperature settings. Want per-request decision, not per-model static choice.
- Must be cheap and robust: use coarse-grain predictors (prompt category, expected length, user tier) and a small set of precomputed sensitivity curves from evaluation harness.

Definitions: (keep simple)
- UPT (utility per token): numeric score reflecting expected business value of a single generated token produced at reference fidelity. Higher => prefer higher quality.
- DeltaQuality(q): expected quality drop (0..1) when using quant level q vs baseline FP16/FP32, estimated from evals on representative prompt set.
- CostPerToken(q): expected infra cost per token at quant level q (inc. amortized compute & memory margins).
- LatencyMultiplier(q): ratio of p95 latency at q divided by baseline. Use to enforce latency SLO constraints.

Scoring formula (simple, transparent):
UPT_effective(q) = UPT_reference * (1 - DeltaQuality(q)) - alpha * (CostPerToken(q) / CostPerToken(baseline))
- UPT_reference = business weight / expected_generated_tokens (we can store as per-request or per-customer)
- alpha = tunable scaling factor to convert dollars into utility units (set by finance/product).
- Decision: choose q* = argmin_q CostPerToken(q) subject to constraints: UPT_effective(q) >= UPT_threshold and LatencyMultiplier(q) <= Latency_limit.

Notes on components: 
- DeltaQuality(q): captured by the "sensitivity curves" tab. For robustness, store median and 90th percentile deltas per prompt-class and per model family. Eg: for long-form narrative, 4-bit median BLEU drop 0.08, 90th pct 0.14. For short factual prompts, INT8 median drop 0.02.
- CostPerToken(q): measured from serving telemetry: include GPU/sec cost, batching benefits, and prefix cache hit adjustments. Tab: "cost sampler" accepts distribution of seq lengths and batch sizes to estimate per-token cost.
- UPT_reference: can be set by product for each route: e.g., "checkout-confirmation" = 10, "chat-ops-short" = 6, "code-gen-long" = 2. This is a compact way to encode business urgency.

Worked example (toy numbers):
Inputs: prompt_class=transactional, expected_tokens=8, UPT_reference=8 (high value), Latency_limit=1.5x, alpha=0.5
Sensitivity (from tab): DeltaQuality(FP8)=0.03, DeltaQuality(INT8)=0.07, DeltaQuality(4bit)=0.18
CostPerToken(baseline FP16)=0.0012, CostPerToken(FP8)=0.0009, CostPerToken(INT8)=0.0006, CostPerToken(4bit)=0.00035
LatencyMultiplier(FP8)=1.0, (INT8)=1.1, (4bit)=1.4
Compute UPT_effective per quant:
- FP8: 8*(1-0.03) - 0.5*(0.0009/0.0012) = 7.76 - 0.375 = 7.385
- INT8: 8*(1-0.07) - 0.5*(0.0006/0.0012) = 7.44 - 0.25 = 7.19
- 4bit: 8*(1-0.18) - 0.5*(0.00035/0.0012) = 6.56 - 0.1458 = 6.4142
If UPT_threshold = 6.5, pick lowest-cost quant satisfying threshold and latency: INT8 passes (7.19 >= 6.5 and latency 1.1x <= 1.5x), 4bit fails. So route to INT8.

Why this is useful:
- Makes tradeoffs explicit (business weight vs dollars).
- Enables different defaults by customer tier: e.g., free-tier UPT_threshold lower.
- Can create hybrid per-request policies: use fallback to higher-fidelity model if output verification fails.

Suggested spreadsheet tabs and columns (sheet layout):
1) config_params (global): alpha, baseline, latency_slos, default_UPT_thresholds per plan.
2) prompt_profile_catalog: prompt_tag, expected_tokens, UPT_reference, typical_temp, model_family, note
3) sensitivity_curves: model_family, prompt_tag, quant_level, median_delta, p90_delta, sample_size, eval_date
4) cost_sampler: quant_level, gpu_type, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, gpcost_per_hour, batch_profile, per_token_estimate
5) simulation: stochastic draws of prompt profiles against sensitivity and cost to compute expected monthly savings and quality regressions
6) routing_rules: if/then style decision table that can be mechanically exported to the router config
7) backtest: past-week actuals mapped to the scoring function to flag misfires (cases where quality regressions exceed tolerance)

Open questions / decisions for next iteration:
- How to set alpha? Options: tie to unit economics (gross margin per token) or derive from customer-level ROI experiments. For early iteration, use a fixed heuristic (0.3-0.6) then tune.
- Safety net: how often should outputs be sampled for quality monitoring? Start with 1/1000 for high-volume routes, 1/100 for critical transactional routes.
- Support for multi-stage pipelines (e.g., generate -> rerank): need composition rules. If first stage is quantized heavily but reranker uses high-fidelity, overall quality effect is non-linear. Add an adjustment factor in sensitivity curves for multi-stage flows.
- Cold-start / unknown prompt_tag: fallback to conservative INT8 or FP8 depending on latency SLOs.

Experiment plan (short):
1) Build sensitivity_curves for 6 prompt_tags x 3 model_families x 4 quant_levels (FP16 baseline, FP8, INT8, 4bit). Use existing eval harness in GH link above. (Owner: Lucia)
2) Instrument cost_sampler from recent batch telemetry (one week) to derive CostPerToken by quant and gpu type. (Owner: Benji)
3) Run simulation on previous two months of traffic to estimate overall token-level savings and predicted quality regressions. (Owner: Omar)
4) Canary routing rules for internal apps (5% traffic), sample outputs to check regression rates, adjust alpha/thresholds.

Operational notes for SDK/Router export:
- Routing rules export format should be compact JSON lines: {prompt_tag, expected_tokens_bucket, plan, quant_level, reason_code}
- Allow per-request override via headers for high-trust customers.

Appendix: quick heuristics cheatsheet (for PM/Eng)
- Short, high-value prompts (<=12 tokens): bias to INT8 if p90 DeltaQuality(INT8) <= 0.1 and latency OK.
- Medium prompts (12-200 tokens): FP8 or INT8 depending on model sensitivity; 4-bit rarely except for cost-first background generation.
- Long-form (>200 tokens): prefer FP8 or FP16 if quality-critical; 4-bit OK for supervised compression/transcoding tasks.

TODOs / next edits:
- plug in real numbers from eval harness; remove toy numbers and record dataset ids.
- add small decision-tree export example usable by router team.
- write short API proposal: headers that SDK can send (prompt_tag, expected_tokens, plan_tier, fidelity_override) and flagging semantics.

Linked tickets / refs: see top linked_artifacts.

Notes to self: keep the scoring function intentionally simple; if we overfit to complicated utility transforms it gets hard to audit in enterprise reviews. The main win is creating interpretable knobs (UPT_threshold, alpha) and a straightforward backtest sheet.
